Long-legged doji.long:
A doji forms when a bar's open and close land at almost the same price, leaving a body close to nothing regardless of how far the bar travelled. The long-legged version adds long wicks on both sides: price pushed well above and well below the open before settling back near it.

Mechanically this records two failed attempts in one bar - buyers drove price up and gave it back, sellers drove it down and gave it back, and neither side held the close. Nothing about the shape says which side wins the next bar; it only records that this one ended in a stalemate.

The doji family has a documented lineage: Japanese rice traders used candle charting centuries before it reached the West, and Steve Nison's 1991 book popularised the vocabulary for English-speaking traders. That history explains the naming, not the reliability of any signal drawn from it.

Where people get fooled: a long-legged doji at the top of a chart looks dramatic, and hindsight makes the "reversal" look obvious. In real time the same shape appears constantly inside ranges that go nowhere, and nobody screenshots those.
Long-legged doji.usage: Used to flag a bar where price tested both directions and closed roughly where it opened, prompting traders to wait for the next bar before reading direction.

Dragonfly doji.long:
A dragonfly doji has its open, high and close bunched at the top of the bar, with a long lower wick underneath. It only forms when sellers pushed price well below the open and buyers took all of it back by the close.

The shape is a single-bar record of a rejected low: whoever was selling into that move failed to hold it, and the bar closed at its high. It says nothing about what buyers do with that information next.

Because the open and close sit at the same level as the high, a dragonfly doji is really a hammer-shaped bar with an almost non-existent body - the naming split exists mostly for Japanese candlestick vocabulary, not a separate mechanism.

Where people get fooled: the long wick reads as unambiguous buyer strength, but a wick this size can equally mean the bar caught a stop run or a thin patch of liquidity, and the next bar frequently gives back the whole recovery.
Dragonfly doji.usage: Read as a rejected low within a single bar, and typically checked against the bars either side before it's treated as more than noise.

Gravestone doji.long:
A gravestone doji is the mirror of the dragonfly: open, low and close bunch at the bottom of the bar, with a long upper wick above. Buyers pushed price well above the open and gave all of it back by the close.

Structurally it's a shooting-star-shaped bar with almost no body - a failed push higher recorded in one candle, nothing more. The name describes the shape, not an outcome for the next bar.

Its meaning depends entirely on where it sits: printed after a long advance it gets read as exhaustion, printed inside a sideways range it usually gets ignored, even though the candle itself is identical in both cases.

Where people get fooled: the same bar shape shows up constantly during normal chop, but only the ones at chart extremes get pointed to afterwards, which makes gravestones look like a top-calling tool they were never shown to be.
Gravestone doji.usage: Marked as a rejected high within a single bar, most often discussed at the top of an extended move rather than in the middle of a range.

Marubozu.long:
A marubozu is a candle with no wicks, or next to none: the open sits at the high or low and the close sits at the other extreme, so the full body spans the bar's entire range.

That shape means one side controlled the bar from the opening trade to the closing trade, with no meaningful pushback recorded at any point in between. A bullish marubozu opens at the low and closes at the high; a bearish one does the reverse.

It's one of the oldest candle shapes in the Japanese charting tradition that Steve Nison brought to English-language trading literature, and it remains the simplest one: there's no ambiguity about where the open and close sat relative to the range.

Where people get fooled: an unbroken body looks like conviction, but a single bar of one-sided control says nothing about whether that control continues. Wide-range marubozu bars are also common around scheduled news, where the range reflects a repricing event rather than sustained directional flow.
Marubozu.usage: Used to describe a bar where one side held control from open to close without a meaningful pullback recorded inside it.

Hanging man.long:
A hanging man has a small body near the top of its range with a long lower wick and little or no upper wick, appearing after an uptrend. Sellers pushed price down during the bar before buyers pulled it back to close near the open.

The shape is identical to a hammer; the only difference is the context it appears in - a hammer sits after a decline, a hanging man sits after an advance, and traders read the same candle two different ways depending on that placement.

The lower wick shows demand appeared at some point in the bar, but a small body near the highs also means sellers were active enough to drag price down first, which is why this one gets treated as a caution sign rather than a hammer's more hopeful read.

Where people get fooled: naming a shape after its position rather than after anything it measures means the label gets added in hindsight. The bar looks the same whether the next move confirms the caution or ignores it entirely.
Hanging man.usage: Noted after an advance as a bar where sellers showed up intraday even though buyers pulled the close back up, usually read alongside the next bar rather than alone.

Shooting star.long:
A shooting star has a small body near the bottom of its range with a long upper wick, appearing after an uptrend. Price pushed well above the open during the bar, then sellers took it back down to close near where it started.

The wick records a failed push higher; the small body near the low shows that failure held into the close rather than being partially recovered. On its own that's the entire fact set the bar provides.

Same shape as a gravestone doji if the body shrinks to nearly nothing, and identical in construction to an inverted hammer - only the preceding trend differs, which is what determines the name applied and the reading that follows.

Where people get fooled: a long upper wick after a rally photographs well as a top, but the same wick shape appears throughout an uptrend without marking a turn most of the time - it's only remembered when it happens to be followed by one.
Shooting star.usage: Read after an advance as a bar where an intraday push higher was fully rejected by the close, typically weighed against volume and the following bar.

Inverted hammer.long:
An inverted hammer has a small body near the bottom of its range with a long upper wick, appearing after a downtrend. It is the same shape as a shooting star; only the direction of the prior move differs.

The wick shows buyers pushed price up during the bar before it settled back down, which some read as early interest emerging even though the close didn't hold near the high.

Because the bar closes near its low despite the upward push, it's a weaker signal by construction than a bar that closes near its high - the "inverted hammer" name borrows the hammer's more hopeful reputation for a candle that actually finished on the back foot.

Where people get fooled: the label implies kinship with the hammer's stronger close-near-high shape, but the two candles resolve very differently, and treating them as equivalent because they share half a name is a naming trap rather than a market one.
Inverted hammer.usage: Discussed after a decline as a bar showing an intraday push higher that failed to hold into the close, often paired with the following bar before it's treated as meaningful.

Pin bar.long:
A pin bar is a candle with a small body and one long wick pointing away from a tested level, with little or no wick on the opposite side. The name comes from price-action trading communities rather than the original Japanese candlestick vocabulary.

Mechanically it describes exactly the same construction as a hammer, shooting star, hanging man or inverted hammer - the wick shows a level was probed and rejected within the bar. "Pin bar" is a generic label applied regardless of where in a trend the bar sits.

Because it collapses several named candlestick shapes into one looser category, exactly how long a wick has to be and how small a body has to be to qualify is left to whoever is drawing the box around it.

Where people get fooled: the term sounds like a distinct discovery, but it's a repackaging of older candlestick shapes under a name popular in retail price-action courses, and the lack of a fixed definition means two traders can disagree on whether the same bar qualifies.
Pin bar.usage: Used across price-action trading communities as a catch-all label for a rejection candle, without a single fixed rule for how long the wick must be.

Bearish engulfing.long:
A bearish engulfing pattern is two candles: an up candle followed by a down candle whose body fully covers the prior body, opening above the first candle's close and closing below its open.

It records a full reversal of control within one extra bar - whatever buying pushed the first candle up gets more than matched by selling on the second. The larger the second body relative to the first, the more complete that reversal looks.

The bullish version works the same way at lows; the umbrella term "engulfing" covers both directions, and the pattern is one of the more mechanically precise shapes in the candlestick set, because the rule - body fully covers body - is unambiguous compared with wick-based patterns.

Where people get fooled: precise construction doesn't mean predictive power - a clean two-bar reversal in body size says nothing about whether the move that follows continues, and engulfing bars appear constantly inside ranges that never turn into trends.
Bearish engulfing.usage: Identified where a candle's body fully covers the prior candle's body in the opposite direction, typically checked against the wider trend before it's read as a turn.

Harami.long:
A harami is two candles where the second candle's entire body sits inside the first candle's body - the opposite construction to an engulfing pattern. The word is Japanese for "pregnant," describing the smaller candle nested inside the larger one.

The shape records a sharp contraction in range and conviction: whatever drove the first bar's wide body didn't repeat, and the market compressed instead. That's a statement about momentum slowing, not necessarily about direction reversing.

A harami with a very small second body, close to a doji, is sometimes given its own name in older texts, though the underlying mechanism - one candle nested inside the other - stays the same either way.

Where people get fooled: contraction after a big bar happens constantly and most of the time simply precedes more of the same trend, a pause rather than a reversal, so treating every harami as an early warning overstates what a shrinking range actually tells you.
Harami.usage: Noted as a sharp contraction where the second candle's body sits fully inside the first, discussed as a pause in momentum rather than a confirmed turn.

Inside bar.long:
An inside bar has its entire range - high and low, not just the body - contained within the prior bar's range. It's a range-based definition, unlike harami, which is defined by candle bodies.

The shape marks a contraction in volatility for that period: whatever pushed the prior bar wider didn't repeat, and price stayed contained inside the older extremes. On its own it says nothing about which way the range eventually resolves.

What counts as an inside bar is timeframe-relative - a contraction on a one-hour chart can sit anywhere inside a single daily bar and be invisible at that higher timeframe, so the same stretch of price can be described as compressing or not depending purely on which chart it's viewed on.

Where people get fooled: a tight inside bar looks like coiled energy about to release, but plenty of inside bars just sit inside a wider consolidation and get followed by another inside bar, not a breakout.
Inside bar.usage: Used to flag a bar whose full range sits inside the prior bar's range, generally discussed as a contraction rather than a directional signal on its own.

Outside bar.long:
An outside bar has a range - high and low - that fully covers the prior bar's range on both sides. It's the range-based mirror of an inside bar, and often confused with the body-based engulfing pattern despite being a different construction.

Because it's defined by wicks and body together rather than body alone, an outside bar can occur without qualifying as an engulfing candle, and an engulfing candle can occur without its range fully covering the prior bar - the two labels overlap but aren't interchangeable.

The shape shows a wider net of prices traded in one bar than in the one before it, which some read as a volatility expansion worth paying attention to regardless of which direction the bar closed.

Where people get fooled: "outside bar" and "engulfing bar" get used interchangeably in casual chat even though the rules differ, and mixing the definitions means a trader can believe two signals confirmed each other when only one of them actually fired.
Outside bar.usage: Flagged where a bar's full range exceeds the prior bar's range on both sides, often confused in casual use with the body-based engulfing pattern.

Morning star.long:
A morning star is a three-candle bottom pattern: a long down candle, a small-bodied candle that gaps or nearly gaps lower, then a long up candle that closes well into the first candle's body.

The middle candle is the key piece - its small body shows the selling from the first candle stalled, and the third candle shows buying stepped in hard enough to erase a large part of the decline in one bar.

The "gap" between candles that the classic definition describes is a feature of markets that close overnight, such as stocks; in continuously traded markets like forex or crypto the pattern usually shows up as a small-bodied candle without a true gap, and traders adapt the definition accordingly.

Where people get fooled: three specific candles in a row is a demanding sequence to define precisely, and how "small" the middle body has to be, or how far the third candle has to close into the first, is left to the person drawing the pattern after they already know what happened next.
Morning star.usage: Identified as a three-candle sequence - decline, stall, strong recovery - discussed as a bottoming shape rather than a confirmed reversal on its own.

Evening star.long:
An evening star is the mirror top pattern: a long up candle, a small-bodied candle that gaps or nearly gaps higher, then a long down candle that closes well into the first candle's body.

The middle candle again does the interpretive work - its small body shows the prior buying stalled, and the third candle shows selling arrived hard enough to erase a large part of the advance.

Like the morning star, the gap-based version comes from markets that close overnight; on instruments that trade continuously the pattern typically appears without a true gap, just a small body sandwiched between two larger ones in opposite directions.

Where people get fooled: the three-candle shape is memorable and easy to point to after the fact, but exactly where the "small" middle body ends and exactly how far the third candle needs to close back are choices, not fixed rules, and different chartists draw them differently on the same chart.
Evening star.usage: Identified as a three-candle sequence - advance, stall, strong reversal down - discussed as a topping shape rather than confirmation of a turn.

Three white soldiers.long:
Three white soldiers is a run of three consecutive long-bodied up candles, each opening within the previous candle's body and closing near its own high, with limited wicks on either end.

The repetition is the point: three bars of sustained one-directional control in a row is a stronger statement of momentum than any single wide-range candle, because it rules out a single-bar spike caused by a one-off order or news print.

How "long-bodied" and "near its high" get defined is not fixed - a looser reading will flag sequences a stricter reading would reject, so two people scanning the same chart can disagree on where a valid run starts and ends.

Where people get fooled: three strong up bars in a row looks like proof of a trend taking hold, but a run that long is also exactly what a sharp, short-lived squeeze looks like before it gives the gains back just as quickly.
Three white soldiers.usage: Used to describe three consecutive strong up candles as a sign of sustained buying pressure rather than a single spike.

Three black crows.long:
Three black crows is the mirror pattern: three consecutive long-bodied down candles, each opening within the previous candle's body and closing near its own low.

As with the bullish version, the value of the pattern lies in the repetition - three consecutive bars under one-directional control is read as more significant than a single sharp drop, since it removes a one-off spike as the explanation.

The pattern requires a judgement call on how strictly "long-bodied" and "near its low" apply, and a looser standard catches more sequences than a strict one, which means the pattern's frequency depends heavily on whoever is counting rather than on any fixed, published rule.

Where people get fooled: a run of three red candles reads as capitulation setting in, but the same shape also describes the middle of an orderly, unremarkable decline that keeps going for another ten bars afterwards without any reversal at all showing up.
Three black crows.usage: Used to describe three consecutive strong down candles as a sign of sustained selling pressure rather than a single spike.

Tweezer top / bottom.long:
A tweezer top is two or more candles that share almost the same high; a tweezer bottom is two or more that share almost the same low, regardless of what each candle's body looks like.

The pattern is really about the wicks lining up, not about the bodies - the shared extreme shows a specific price was tested more than once in a row and held both times, unlike a single wick which only records one test.

How close two highs or lows need to be to count as "matching" is not standardised - a strict reading requires near-identical prices, a loose reading allows a small tolerance band, and the tolerance chosen changes how often the pattern appears on the same chart.

Where people get fooled: a level tested twice looks more significant than a level tested once, but two tests in quick succession can just as easily mean the level is about to give way on the third attempt as that it's holding.
Tweezer top / bottom.usage: Flagged where two or more candles share a near-identical high or low, read as a level being tested and held more than once.

Piercing line.long:
A piercing line is a two-candle bottom pattern: a down candle followed by an up candle that opens below the first candle's low and closes above the midpoint of the first candle's body, without closing above the first candle's open.

That "above the midpoint, but not above the open" rule is what separates it from a bullish engulfing pattern - a piercing line is a strong partial recovery, but not a full reversal of the prior bar's body within a single candle.

Its top mirror is dark cloud cover, using the same midpoint rule in the opposite direction; both patterns depend on a precise read of where the "midpoint" of the first candle's body actually sits, which is straightforward on a clean chart and much less so on a noisy one.

Where people get fooled: the midpoint threshold sounds exact, but eyeballing halfway up a candle body on a screen introduces exactly the kind of small measurement disagreement that turns a valid pattern into an invalid one depending on who is looking.
Piercing line.usage: Identified where a recovery candle closes back above the halfway point of the prior down candle's body without fully reversing it.

Dark cloud cover.long:
Dark cloud cover is the top mirror of a piercing line: an up candle followed by a down candle that opens above the first candle's high and closes below the midpoint of the first candle's body, without closing below the first candle's open.

Like the piercing line, the "past the midpoint but not past the open" boundary is what makes it a partial reversal rather than a full engulfing pattern - meaningful selling showed up, but not enough within that one bar to erase the whole prior advance.

The gap-up open used in the classic definition is common on gapping markets like stocks and less common on continuously traded instruments, where the pattern usually shows up as a strong open near the prior high rather than a true gap.

Where people get fooled: naming a candle "dark cloud" primes the reader to expect a top, but a partial pullback into a bar's body happens throughout ordinary uptrends, and most of those don't mark anything more than a pause.
Dark cloud cover.usage: Identified where a reversal candle closes back below the halfway point of the prior up candle's body without fully reversing it.

Spinning top.long:
A spinning top has a small real body with wicks on both sides that are noticeably longer than the body but not extreme - it sits between a full-bodied marubozu and a near-bodyless doji on the same spectrum.

The shape shows both sides of the market were active during the bar - price moved up and down by a meaningful amount - but neither side could hold the close away from where it opened.

Where exactly a candle stops being a "spinning top" and starts being a doji, or stops being a spinning top and becomes an ordinary indecisive candle, is not fixed by any single rule; it's a judgement about proportions that different chartists draw differently.

Where people get fooled: a spinning top at a chart extreme gets read as exhaustion, the same shape in the middle of a trend gets ignored entirely, even though the bar records exactly the same fact - a contested bar that ended near its open - in both places.
Spinning top.usage: Used to describe a candle with a small body and meaningful wicks on both sides, read as a contested, indecisive bar.

Rejection.long:
Rejection describes what a long wick records: price traded away from a level within a bar, then got pushed back before the close, leaving the wick as the only trace of the attempt.

It's the mechanical building block underneath most single-candle patterns - hammers, shooting stars, dojis with long wicks, pin bars - all of them are really just different labels for the same underlying event: a level tested and not held.

The size of a wick that counts as "rejection" rather than ordinary noise is not fixed; a small pullback into the close happens on most bars in any market, and calling all of it rejection would make the term meaningless.

Where people get fooled: a long wick at a round number or a prior high feels like proof the level matters, but wicks of similar length occur constantly at levels nobody was watching, and only the ones near an interesting price get remembered as significant.
Rejection.usage: Used to describe a wick showing price tested and failed to hold a level within a single bar, discussed as a building block of several candle shapes.

Indecision.long:
Indecision describes a bar where the close lands close to the open despite meaningful movement during the bar - the defining trait of dojis and spinning tops. Neither side controlled the close, regardless of what happened in between.

On its own an indecisive bar records only that fact: a contested period. It doesn't specify which side wins the next bar, and reading direction into it requires information outside the candle itself, such as the trend leading into it or the level it formed at.

Indecision is a matter of degree rather than a binary state - a body that's ten per cent of the range and a body that's forty per cent of the range both qualify as "small" to different chartists, which is why the same bar gets classified differently across sources.

Where people get fooled: a run of "indecisive" bars in a tight range is completely ordinary and usually just means volume or interest is low, not that a decisive move is building - most quiet periods stay quiet for longer than expected.
Indecision.usage: Used to describe a bar or cluster of bars where the close sits near the open despite intrabar movement, read alongside context rather than alone.

Volume confirmation.long:
Volume confirmation is the idea that a candlestick or chart pattern carries more weight when it forms on above-average volume - the reasoning being that a move backed by more participation is less likely to be a thin, easily reversed print.

The logic is intuitive but hard to apply cleanly on retail platforms: most forex and CFD brokers display tick volume, a count of price changes, rather than true traded volume, and true volume itself varies by venue for the same instrument.

Even where genuine volume data exists, such as on listed equities or futures, there's no fixed threshold for what counts as "confirming" - a chartist decides in hindsight whether a given volume bar was high enough to matter.

Where people get fooled: adding "confirmed by volume" to a pattern description sounds like an extra layer of rigour, but without a threshold set before the pattern formed, it's just another after-the-fact detail selected because it fits the story already being told.
Volume confirmation.usage: Used to describe checking whether a candlestick pattern coincided with higher-than-average volume, treated as supporting context rather than a separate signal.

Pattern base rate.long:
Pattern base rate is the actual frequency with which a named candlestick or chart shape appears in a market, and separately, the frequency with which whatever "expected" outcome follows it. Neither figure is tracked or published by most retail material that teaches the shapes.

Establishing a base rate requires a fixed, mechanical definition applied consistently across a dataset before looking at outcomes - exactly the discipline candlestick teaching materials skip, since they show hand-picked historical examples rather than every instance a rule would have flagged.

Whoever is identifying a pattern on a chart is usually also the one deciding whether it "worked," using boundaries drawn with the outcome already visible, which inflates the apparent hit rate of almost any shape, real or imagined.

Where people get fooled: a handful of clean chart examples feels like evidence, but a small, curated sample says nothing about how the pattern performs across every instance in the data, including the many that got quietly ignored because they didn't confirm the story.
Pattern base rate.usage: Used to describe the actual, measured frequency of a pattern and its outcomes, as distinct from a handful of remembered examples.

Head and shoulders.long:
A head and shoulders is a three-peak reversal shape: a left shoulder, a higher head, and a right shoulder that roughly matches the left shoulder's height, with a neckline drawn through the two troughs between them.

The pattern is one of the oldest in Western technical analysis, systematised by Richard Schabacker in the 1930s and canonised in Robert Edwards and John Magee's 1948 "Technical Analysis of Stock Trends," which set out most of the classical chart-pattern vocabulary still used today.

A break below the neckline is typically treated as the point the pattern "completes," though the neckline itself can slope, and how far price needs to close below it before the break counts is left to the chartist.

Where people get fooled: three peaks of roughly similar height happen throughout ordinary chop, and it's only once a decline follows that anyone goes back and draws shoulders onto the chart - the pattern is easy to find after the fact and much harder to define in real time.
Head and shoulders.usage: Identified as a three-peak reversal shape with a neckline connecting the troughs, discussed as a shape to watch rather than confirmation of a turn.

Inverse head and shoulders.long:
An inverse head and shoulders is the mirror bottom pattern: a left shoulder, a lower head, and a right shoulder roughly matching the left, with a neckline drawn through the two peaks between them.

It uses the same logic as the top version turned upside down - a break above the neckline is typically treated as the point the pattern completes, with the same ambiguity about how far above and how the neckline's slope should be drawn.

The pattern shares its documented lineage with the standard head and shoulders, part of the classical chart-pattern set formalised by Edwards and Magee rather than a separate later addition to the technical-analysis canon.

Where people get fooled: a bottoming market naturally produces plenty of three-trough sequences, and only the ones followed by an advance get labelled afterwards as a valid inverse head and shoulders - the ones that failed are rarely shown next to them.
Inverse head and shoulders.usage: Identified as a three-trough reversal shape with a neckline connecting the peaks, discussed as a bottoming shape rather than confirmation of a turn.

Neckline.long:
A neckline is the trendline drawn through the two troughs of a head and shoulders, or the two peaks of an inverse version, used as the reference level a break beneath or above is measured against.

It's rarely perfectly horizontal - the two troughs or peaks it connects are seldom at identical prices, so the chartist chooses a slope, and a sloped neckline gives a different "break" price depending on exactly where along it the break is checked.

The neckline also anchors the measured-move target commonly used with the pattern: the vertical distance from the head to the neckline gets projected outward from the break point as an estimate of how far the move might extend.

Where people get fooled: two people looking at the same chart can draw two different necklines depending on which minor wiggle they treat as the "real" trough, which means the exact break price - and whether the pattern has completed at all - is a matter of opinion, not measurement.
Neckline.usage: Used to describe the line connecting a head and shoulders pattern's troughs or peaks, treated as the reference level for a completed break.

Double top.long:
A double top is two peaks at a similar price level with a trough between them, forming a rough "M" shape. A break below the trough is typically treated as the point the pattern completes.

The second peak failing to exceed the first is read as a sign that buying pressure couldn't repeat itself at that level, though the shape is symmetric enough that it can just as easily be an ordinary range with two touches of its upper boundary.

How close the two peaks need to be to count as "similar" is a judgement call - a strict reading requires near-identical highs, a loose one allows a wide tolerance, and the tolerance chosen changes how often the pattern gets flagged on the same chart.

Where people get fooled: two peaks at a similar level happen constantly in ranging markets, most of them followed by more range rather than a breakdown, and the label "double top" tends to get applied only in hindsight, once a decline has already made it look meaningful.
Double top.usage: Identified as two peaks at a similar level with a trough between them, discussed as a possible range boundary rather than confirmation of a top.

Double bottom.long:
A double bottom is the mirror shape: two troughs at a similar price level with a peak between them, forming a rough "W". A break above the peak is typically treated as the point the pattern completes.

The second trough holding at roughly the same level as the first is read as demand reappearing at that price, though as with the double top, the same shape describes an ordinary range bouncing twice off its lower boundary.

The tolerance for how close the two troughs need to be is again a judgement call, and a chart with a loose enough tolerance will always contain more "double bottoms" than one measured strictly.

Where people get fooled: two touches of a low is a thin sample to call a level defended, and most double bottoms that get pointed to were selected because a rally happened to follow - the ones that broke straight through on the second touch simply aren't called double bottoms at all.
Double bottom.usage: Identified as two troughs at a similar level with a peak between them, discussed as a possible range boundary rather than confirmation of a bottom.

Triple top / bottom.long:
A triple top, or bottom, is the same shape as a double top or bottom with a third test of the level instead of two, before price eventually breaks the other way.

A third touch is sometimes read as stronger evidence that a level is defended than a second touch, on the logic that repeated failure to break through says more about supply or demand at that price than a single failed attempt.

The same tolerance and hindsight problems that apply to double tops and bottoms apply here, compounded by an extra requirement: a third peak or trough has to sit close enough to the first two to count, another boundary drawn by the chartist rather than the market.

Where people get fooled: requiring three touches instead of two sounds more rigorous, but it also means the pattern only gets named after the market has already spent longer testing the level - by the time a "triple" is confirmed, much of the move it's meant to anticipate may already be behind it.
Triple top / bottom.usage: Identified as three tests of a similar high or low before a break the other way, discussed as an extended version of the double top or bottom.

Ascending triangle.long:
An ascending triangle is a flat resistance line with a rising support line beneath it, formed by a series of higher lows testing the same overhead level repeatedly.

It's usually discussed in a continuation context - rising lows into a flat ceiling within an existing uptrend are read as persistent buying absorbing supply at one level, more often framed as bullish than a symmetrical triangle, though the geometry alone doesn't fix the direction of the eventual break.

As the two lines converge, the range the price trades in narrows, which is sometimes described as compression building toward a breakout - a description of shrinking range, not a prediction of which way it resolves.

Where people get fooled: a flat top with rising lows can just as easily resolve down through the rising trendline as up through the flat one, and the "ascending" framing primes readers to expect the bullish outcome before the breakout has actually happened.
Ascending triangle.usage: Identified as a flat resistance line met by a series of rising lows, generally discussed within a continuation context rather than as a fixed directional signal.

Descending triangle.long:
A descending triangle is the mirror shape: a flat support line with a falling resistance line above it, formed by a series of lower highs testing the same level beneath.

It's usually discussed as bearish continuation, on the reasoning that repeated lower highs into a flat floor show persistent selling absorbing demand at one level - the same asymmetric framing applied to the ascending version in the opposite direction, borrowed rather than independently derived.

The convergence of the two lines again describes a narrowing range rather than a forecast, and as with the ascending version, nothing in the geometry itself forces the break to go the labelled direction rather than the other way.

Where people get fooled: a flat bottom with falling highs breaks upward often enough that treating the "descending" label as a reliable directional cue overstates what two converging trendlines actually establish about where the next move is headed.
Descending triangle.usage: Identified as a flat support line met by a series of falling highs, generally discussed within a continuation context rather than as a fixed directional signal.

Symmetrical triangle.long:
A symmetrical triangle has two converging trendlines - falling highs above, rising lows below - meeting at a point, unlike the ascending or descending versions where one side stays flat.

Because both boundaries slope toward each other, the pattern doesn't carry the same built-in directional framing as its asymmetric cousins: it describes range compression only, with the eventual breakout direction left genuinely open until it happens.

Some technical-analysis texts still assign it a directional lean based on the trend it forms within, treating it as a continuation pattern of whatever direction preceded it, though that lean is an added assumption rather than something the triangle's shape alone provides on its own terms.

Where people get fooled: because the pattern has no inherent bias, whichever way it breaks gets explained afterwards as though it were expected all along, and the explanation is fitted neatly to the outcome rather than offered honestly in advance of it.
Symmetrical triangle.usage: Identified as two converging trendlines with no flat side, discussed as range compression without a fixed directional bias built into the shape.

Bull flag.long:
A bull flag is a sharp upward move, the pole, followed by a short, shallow, downward-sloping consolidation channel, the flag, typically read as a pause within an uptrend rather than its end.

The flag's channel is usually drawn with two roughly parallel trendlines sloping against the prior move; a break back in the direction of the pole is treated as the point the pattern resumes.

How steep the pole needs to be and how shallow the flag needs to be to qualify are not standardised, so the same consolidation can be labelled a bull flag by one chartist and just an ordinary pullback by another chartist looking at the identical bars.

Where people get fooled: a sharp move followed by a pause is one of the most common shapes in any trending market, which means bull flags that resolve higher and consolidations that quietly turn into reversals look identical while they're still forming.
Bull flag.usage: Identified as a brief downward-sloping consolidation after a sharp advance, discussed as a possible continuation shape rather than confirmation the advance resumes.

Bear flag.long:
A bear flag is the mirror shape: a sharp downward move, the pole, followed by a short, shallow, upward-sloping consolidation channel, the flag, typically read as a pause within a downtrend rather than its end.

As with the bull flag, a break back in the direction of the pole - downward this time - is treated as the pattern's resumption point, using the same two-trendline construction sloped against the prior move.

The same lack of a fixed standard for pole steepness and flag shallowness applies here, meaning what counts as a valid bear flag versus an ordinary bounce is a judgement call rather than a fixed rule.

Where people get fooled: a pause after a sharp decline gets called a bear flag right up until it isn't one, and the label offers no way to distinguish a genuine pause from the start of a larger reversal while it's still in progress.
Bear flag.usage: Identified as a brief upward-sloping consolidation after a sharp decline, discussed as a possible continuation shape rather than confirmation the decline resumes.

Pennant.long:
A pennant is built the same way as a flag - a sharp move, the pole, followed by a consolidation - except the consolidation converges to a point like a small symmetrical triangle instead of running in a parallel channel.

The distinction between a pennant and a flag is purely the shape of the consolidation's boundary lines: converging for a pennant, roughly parallel for a flag. Both are read as continuation patterns following the direction of the pole.

Because the consolidation is small and short by definition, there's limited room to test whether the converging lines are genuine or just the first few bars of a larger, differently shaped pause that hasn't finished forming yet.

Where people get fooled: a pennant is essentially a flag with a different label attached based on a small number of bars, and calling the shape early - before enough bars exist to tell a pennant from a flag from ordinary noise - is common precisely because both are meant to be brief.
Pennant.usage: Identified as a brief, converging consolidation after a sharp move, distinguished from a flag mainly by the shape of its boundary lines.

Rising wedge.long:
A rising wedge has two converging trendlines that both slope upward, with the lower line rising more steeply than the upper one, squeezing the range into a narrowing upward channel.

It's commonly discussed as a bearish shape regardless of whether it appears at the end of an uptrend or inside a downtrend as a corrective bounce, on the reasoning that upward momentum is fading even as price keeps grinding higher within the wedge.

That bearish framing is a convention rather than something forced by the geometry - other texts treat wedge direction as context-dependent, and a rising wedge inside a strong uptrend doesn't automatically behave the same way as one appearing after an extended advance.

Where people get fooled: the "bearish" label gets applied on sight, before the wedge has actually broken either way, which means traders can spend an extended climb waiting for a reversal that a pattern name promised rather than one the price action has shown.
Rising wedge.usage: Identified as two upward-sloping, converging trendlines, commonly discussed as a bearish shape though its eventual break direction isn't fixed by the geometry alone.

Falling wedge.long:
A falling wedge has two converging trendlines that both slope downward, with the upper line falling more steeply than the lower one, squeezing the range into a narrowing downward channel.

It's commonly discussed as a bullish shape by the same logic in reverse: downward momentum fading even as price keeps grinding lower within the wedge, whether the wedge appears after a decline or as a corrective pullback inside an established uptrend.

As with the rising wedge, that bullish label is a convention applied ahead of any actual break, and the wedge's geometry alone doesn't determine which way it eventually resolves, whatever the convention assumes in advance.

Where people get fooled: applying a directional label before the pattern has broken either way primes traders to expect the labelled outcome, and a falling wedge that simply keeps falling further is no less common a result than one that turns around and reverses.
Falling wedge.usage: Identified as two downward-sloping, converging trendlines, commonly discussed as a bullish shape though its eventual break direction isn't fixed by the geometry alone.

Cup and handle.long:
A cup and handle is a rounded bottom, the cup, followed by a smaller, shorter downward drift, the handle, before a breakout above the level the cup started from.

Unlike most of the classical shapes in this section, cup and handle isn't from Edwards and Magee's original canon; it was popularised later by William O'Neil through Investor's Business Daily and the CANSLIM approach, aimed specifically at equities.

The rounded cup is meant to show a gradual shift from selling to buying rather than a sharp reversal, and the handle is read as a final shakeout of weak holders before the breakout - both descriptions applied after the shape is already visible on the chart.

Where people get fooled: "rounded" and "shallow handle" are qualitative descriptions with no fixed measurement, so the pattern can be drawn onto a wide range of price paths that don't closely resemble each other, as long as a rally eventually follows.
Cup and handle.usage: Identified as a rounded bottom followed by a shallow pullback before a breakout, a shape popularised for equities rather than part of the older classical set.

Rounding bottom.long:
A rounding bottom, or saucer, is a gradual, curved reversal from a decline into an advance, without the sharp pivot points that define most other chart patterns.

The slow curve is read as a gradual handover of control - selling pressure easing off bit by bit rather than buyers stepping in all at once - which is also why it's harder to pin down with straight trendlines the way triangles or wedges are.

Because it lacks clean pivot points, a rounding bottom is one of the more subjective shapes to identify: where it starts, where it ends, and how "rounded" is rounded enough are all matters of eyeballing a curve rather than measuring a defined line.

Where people get fooled: a slow, gradual decline that simply keeps declining can look identical to the early stage of a rounding bottom for a long stretch, and the "rounding" label usually only gets applied once the advance that confirms it has already started.
Rounding bottom.usage: Identified as a gradual, curved shift from decline to advance without sharp pivot points, discussed as one of the harder shapes to define precisely.

Channel.long:
A channel is two roughly parallel trendlines bounding price action, one drawn through the highs and one through the lows, containing the swings between them.

Price moving from one boundary toward the other is read as the channel "working," and a close beyond either line is typically treated as a potential break, though channels can also simply widen or tilt gradually without any clean break occurring.

Because both lines are drawn through a chosen set of swing points, a channel's angle and width change depending on which highs and lows the chartist selects to anchor it, and a channel can usually be redrawn several slightly different ways on the same chart.

Where people get fooled: a channel that has held for a long stretch feels like a fixed structure, but every touch that stays inside it is really just the most recent point in a series that could break at any time, and past adherence to the lines doesn't extend their hold into the future.
Channel.usage: Used to describe price bounded between two roughly parallel trendlines, with moves between the boundaries and breaks beyond them both discussed as chart features.

Broadening formation.long:
A broadening formation, sometimes called a megaphone, is the opposite of a triangle: two trendlines diverging rather than converging, with each swing extending further from the last than the one before it.

The widening range is read as a sign of increasing disagreement between buyers and sellers - each attempt to push a level fails by a larger margin than the last, rather than compressing toward a single resolution point.

Because the swings keep extending outward, a broadening formation is harder to trade around than a converging pattern: there's no narrowing apex forcing a resolution, and the pattern can keep widening for an extended stretch before anything resembling a breakout occurs.

Where people get fooled: a widening range looks unstable and dramatic, which invites a story about an approaching climax, but a broadening formation has no built-in end point the way a converging triangle does, and the widening alone doesn't say when, or whether, it stops.
Broadening formation.usage: Identified as two diverging trendlines with progressively larger swings, discussed as increasing range instability rather than a pattern with a defined resolution point.

Measured move.long:
A measured move is a projection technique: the size of a completed price move - often the pole of a flag, or the head-to-neckline distance of a head and shoulders - is measured and then re-applied from a breakout point to estimate a target.

It's simple arithmetic dressed up as a forecast: take a known distance, project it forward from a new reference point, and call the result a target. Nothing about the method draws on anything beyond that one measured distance.

Different practitioners measure from different anchor points - the breakout candle's open, its close, the exact neckline touch - so the same pattern can generate several different "measured move" targets depending on which anchor is chosen.

Where people get fooled: a specific-looking number produced by measuring a chart feels more rigorous than a round guess, but the arithmetic doesn't carry any information about whether price actually reaches that level - it only restates the size of the move that already happened.
Measured move.usage: Used to describe projecting a completed move's size forward from a breakout point as an arithmetic estimate, not a forecast derived from anything beyond that measurement.

Throwback / pullback to the breakout.long:
A throwback, or pullback, to the breakout is price returning to retest a level it just broke through, before - if it does - resuming in the direction of the original break.

Some traders wait deliberately for this retest before entering, on the logic that the broken level should now act as support or resistance from the other side, and a hold there offers confirmation the breakout wasn't a false one.

The retest doesn't always happen, and when it does happen it doesn't always hold - price can throw back to the level, fail to hold it, and reverse straight back through, which erases the very confirmation the retest was meant to provide.

Where people get fooled: waiting for a throwback assumes one turns up, and moves that never look back happen often enough that a rule requiring a retest before acting misses those moves entirely while offering no real protection on the ones that do throw back and fail.
Throwback / pullback to the breakout.usage: Used to describe price returning to a just-broken level before continuing, discussed as one possible path among several rather than a required step after a breakout.

Retest.long:
A retest is price returning to a specific level - a broken trendline, a prior high or low, a neckline - after moving away from it, to see whether the level now behaves differently than it did before.

The general logic is that a level which acted as resistance can flip to support once broken, or vice versa, and a retest is the moment that flip gets checked against actual trading rather than assumed.

The term applies across almost every pattern in this section - triangles, flags, head and shoulders, double tops - because nearly any broken line or level can be retested, which makes it one of the more general-purpose words in chart-pattern vocabulary.

Where people get fooled: a retest that holds gets remembered as proof the level mattered, and a retest that fails gets quietly reclassified as a false breakout instead, so the same event ends up supporting whichever story is told about it after the fact.
Retest.usage: Used to describe price returning to a previously broken level to check whether it now holds from the other side.

False breakout.long:
A false breakout is a break of a level - a trendline, a range boundary, a pattern's neckline - that reverses back through the level shortly after, rather than continuing in the direction of the break.

It's identical in construction to a genuine breakout while it's happening; the only thing that distinguishes the two is what price does afterwards, which means there's no way to tell them apart from the break candle alone.

The term overlaps heavily with "fakeout" and with stop-hunt narratives - a false breakout that clears a level just far enough to trigger stop orders before reversing is often described using both terms interchangeably, even though "false breakout" only describes the outcome, not the cause.

Where people get fooled: calling a break "false" only after it reverses is a description applied in hindsight, and a trading rule built to filter out false breakouts in advance is, by construction, also filtering out some genuine ones that happened to look identical before they resolved.
False breakout.usage: Used to describe a break of a level that reverses shortly after, a label that only gets applied once the reversal has already happened.

Trendline.long:
A trendline is a straight line connecting two or more swing points - highs for a downtrend line, lows for an uptrend line - used as a simple visual reference for the angle of a move.

It's the most basic drawing tool in chart analysis and also one of the most subjective: a trendline needs at least two points to draw and a third to "confirm," but which swing points count as valid touches is entirely up to whoever is drawing it.

Extending a trendline forward projects it as a level for future price to react to, though nothing about drawing a line through past points obliges price to respect it going forward - the line is a description of what already happened, extrapolated.

Where people get fooled: a trendline that's been touched several times looks like an established rule the market is following, but a line can usually be angled slightly differently to hit a different set of touches just as well, and the version that "worked" is the one that gets kept on the chart.
Trendline.usage: Used to describe a line drawn through two or more swing points, treated as a reference for the angle of a move rather than a fixed rule price must follow.

Pattern subjectivity.long:
Pattern subjectivity is the general problem underlying every shape in this section: chart patterns require boundary choices - where a neckline sits, whether a spike counts as a shoulder, how flat "flat" resistance needs to be - that aren't fixed by any external rule.

Two chartists working from the same price history can draw two different versions of the same pattern, both defensible, because the underlying method - draw lines through the swing points that look right - doesn't specify in advance which points qualify.

This is distinct from a candlestick pattern's more mechanical rules, such as engulfing's body-covers-body test - chart patterns lean much more heavily on visual judgement, which is part of why the same historical chart can be shown as evidence for several contradictory patterns depending on which lines get drawn.

Where people get fooled: a chart pattern illustrated in a book or course always looks clean because the example was chosen for clarity after the fact; identifying the same pattern in real time, before the outcome is known, involves far more ambiguous swing points than the textbook version ever shows.
Pattern subjectivity.usage: Used to describe the boundary and anchor-point choices every chart pattern requires, which is why the same price history can be drawn as more than one valid pattern.
